claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy has an intact, passivating oxide film.
The oxide film was developed under processing conditions optimized for wear and corrosion resistance.
Increasing mechanical wear or applied load damages or removes the protective oxide film.
Removal of the oxide film exposes fresh underlying alloy.
Freshly exposed alloy corrodes faster than the film-covered surface.
Corrosion of the exposed surface impedes effective reformation of the protective film.
Film removal, accelerated corrosion, and inhibited film reformation form a positive degradation feedback loop.
The proposed feedback loop synergistically increases overall degradation.
Increasing applied mechanical load increases wear relative to a static or minimally loaded baseline.
Increasing applied mechanical load accelerates corrosion relative to a static or minimally loaded baseline in the same corrosive environment.
Increasing applied mechanical load increases total degradation relative to the baseline.
A static or minimally loaded control retains a more intact oxide film.
The prediction should hold when corrosion kinetics depend significantly on film integrity and the film is substantially protective at low load.
Exceptionally rapid self-healing of the oxide film may suppress the predicted load-dependent degradation.
A corrosive medium that is too mild to affect film dynamics may suppress the predicted response.
The magnitudes of the corrosion and wear increases depend on alloy composition and environmental aggressiveness.
Holding chemical exposure constant while varying the mechanical condition is intended to isolate the effect of mechanical loading.

contradictions.description: The comparison is described as varying only mechanical load, but sliding speed and normal force are offered interchangeably as load variables. Sliding speed is not mechanical load and can independently change contact time, frictional heating, mass transport, and electrochemical behavior, so the stated one-variable control is internally inconsistent unless speed and force are tested separately.
